$comment: Every file in this directory must keep being refused by plugin API 0.1.
`stage` records WHERE the refusal happens, because that distinction is part of the
contract: `manifest` means PluginManifest::parse rejects it outright, while
`capability-grant` means the manifest is well-formed but CapabilitySet::resolve refuses
it at install time. An author debugging the second one is not looking at a syntax error.
`messageContains` is asserted case-insensitively so wording can be improved without
breaking the fixture; the code and the stage are the parts that must not drift.

replacement-uses-a-custom-frame.json.why: A replacement is the whole screen. The host-rendered path is themed, accessible and controller-navigable by construction; a custom frame owns all of that itself and is still a prototype, so standing one in for a built-in surface is building a product on unproven ground.

replacement-names-an-unknown-surface.jso.why: Replaceable surfaces are a closed set so that renaming an internal component is not a breaking change for plugins. A manifest naming one this build does not have must fail rather than be silently ignored, or the author sees a plugin that installs and does nothing.

two-offers-for-one-surface.json.why: One plugin offering the same surface twice would appear in the user's picker as two entries they cannot tell apart by origin, which makes the choice meaningless.

activation-names-nothing.json.why: An activation event pointing at a missing contribution never fires, which reads to the author as 'my plugin does nothing'.

contribution-id-with-separator.json.why: `/` is the namespace separator the host adds; an author using one produces an id that cannot be parsed back into (plugin, local).

depends-on-itself.json.why: The shortest possible cycle, caught before resolution ever runs.

duplicate-command-id.json.why: A plugin colliding with itself is an author mistake worth naming precisely.

entrypoint-escapes-package.json.why: Path traversal is refused in the contract, so the same rule holds for a development folder that is never extracted from anything.

entrypoint-is-typescript.json.why: TypeScript is compiled at packaging time; the launcher is not a build tool.

hosts-without-network-capability.json.why: Hosts with no capability is a permission the user was never asked about.

id-without-publisher.json.why: The publisher segment is the namespace that lets two people both write `dashboard` with no registry to arbitrate.

insecure-source-url.json.why: The manager shows this link prominently; a plaintext one is worth refusing.

misspelled-field.json.why: `deny_unknown_fields`, so a typo fails loudly instead of producing a plugin that mysteriously does nothing.

network-capability-without-hosts.json.why: A network capability with no hosts can never do anything, so it is a mistake rather than a minimal request.

network-ip-literal.json.why: An IP literal sidesteps DNS, and with it the private-range rejection that protects the user's own network.

network-wildcard-host.json.why: `*.example.com` is not something a user can evaluate at an install prompt.

script-contribution-without-entrypoint.j.why: A command with nothing to call into would be dead on arrival.

unknown-manifest-schema.json.why: A manifest for a schema this host does not know is refused rather than guessed at.

unknown-required-capability.json.why: Well-formed, but asks for something this API version cannot provide. The honest answer is 'this Agora is too old', not 'permission denied' — so it is an API incompatibility, and it surfaces at grant time rather than at parse time.
